overview:
Antakrddasa (Prakrit: *Antagadadasā*, Sanskrit: *Antakṛddasha*) is one of the twelve canonical *āgamas* of the Śvetāmbara Jain tradition. It belongs to the group of *Prakīrṇaka* texts—shorter scriptures that address specific doctrinal or narrative themes. The Antakrddasa focuses on the lives of individuals who attained liberation (*mokṣa*) by destroying the final remnants of karmic bondage, specifically the *antarāya* (obstructive) karmas. Its narratives illustrate how laypeople and ascetics, through intense spiritual effort, right faith, and ethical discipline, reached the state of *kevala-jñāna* (omniscience) and ultimately *nirvāṇa*.

The text is structured as a collection of exemplary biographies. Each story highlights the final stages of spiritual progress, emphasizing the destruction of karmas, the cultivation of equanimity, and the relinquishing of attachment. These accounts serve as moral and devotional models for practitioners, illustrating how liberation is possible even for individuals living in complex worldly circumstances. The Antakrddasa is frequently studied in conjunction with other narrative āgamas such as the *Vipākaśruta* and *Jñātadharmakathā*, which also explore karmic fruition and spiritual transformation.

Within the broader Jain scriptural tradition, the Antakrddasa is significant for its detailed portrayal of the *antakṛt*—those who have “made an end” to the cycle of rebirth. It provides insight into the final stages of the *guṇasthāna* ladder, especially the transition from advanced spiritual states to liberation. While Digambara traditions do not preserve this text in their canonical corpus, parallel themes appear in Digambara narrative literature, demonstrating shared doctrinal foundations across sects.

Modern scholarship views the Antakrddasa as an important source for understanding early Jain narrative style, karmic theory, and the pedagogical use of exemplars. Its stories continue to be used in contemporary Jain education to illustrate the lived path toward liberation, while commentarial traditions highlight the text’s doctrinal precision and ethical depth.

primary_sources.title: Antakrddasa (Antagadadasā)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to the disciples of Mahāvīra; compiled within the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: अंतकृद्दश (sample verse): "एवं मे सुयक्खं तं समयं, जहा अंतेकडो होइ"
primary_sources.transliteration: evaṃ me suyakkhaṃ taṃ samayaṃ, jahā antekaḍo hoi
primary_sources.translation: “Thus have I heard: at that time, one becomes an ‘ender’ of the cycle (antakṛt).”
primary_sources.notes: This line represents the narrative formula typical of Śvetāmbara canonical texts. The Antakrddasa consists of accounts of individuals who destroyed the final karmas. The canonical text is preserved in the Śvetāmbara *Dvādaśāṅgī* tradition, with commentaries by Haribhadra and later scholastics.

misconceptions.myth: The Antakrddasa is a Digambara canonical scripture.
misconceptions.reality: The Antakrddasa belongs specifically to the Śvetāmbara canon. Digambara traditions do not include it in their canonical list, though similar themes appear in Digambara narrative literature.

misconceptions.myth: The text describes only monks attaining liberation.
misconceptions.reality: The Antakrddasa includes accounts of both laypeople and ascetics who destroyed the final karmas, illustrating that liberation is accessible to individuals in varied life situations.

misconceptions.myth: The stories are purely mythological and have no doctrinal significance.
misconceptions.reality: The narratives are doctrinally structured to illustrate karmic destruction, advanced *guṇasthānas*, and the ethical path toward liberation. They serve as pedagogical tools within Jain spiritual instruction.
